item.title: Methods for Assessing Distributional Assumptions in Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.03333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies is commonly based on bivariate generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) that assume normally distributed study-specific random effects. In practice, this distributional assumption is rarely examined, particularly in individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA), where empirical Bayes (EB) estimates exhibit heterogeneous precision across studies. Applying standard multivariate normality tests to such estimates can therefore lead to misleading inference. We propose a weighted extension of the Henze-Zirkler (HZ) test to assess bivariate normality of random effects, accounting for study-specific precision via inverse-variance weighting. To obtain valid finite-sample inference, we develop a parametric bootstrap calibration procedure. Extensive simulation studies showed that the classical HZ test applied to EB estimates can exhibit substantial Type I error inflation, whereas the proposed weighted procedures maintain nominal error rates while retaining power to detect departures from normality. The proposed method provides a practical, statistically principled diagnostic tool for assessing random-effects distributional assumptions in hierarchical models, with particular relevance to IPDMA of DTA studies. Although motivated by IPDMA, the proposed approach also extends to aggregate-data diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis based on study-level 2-by-2 tables.
item.dc:creator: Diribsa T. Bedada, Zelalem F. Negeri

item.title: Evaluation of clinical prediction models: Decomposing performance uncertainty into model development and validation components
item.description: arXiv:2611.03337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There has been growing emphasis on acknowledging, quantifying, and communicating the uncertainty inherent in the output of clinical prediction models. However, allowing for model uncertainty when assessing the performance of an existing model in a new sample (i.e., external validation) has not been sufficiently explored. When validating a model that generates uncertain predictions, the uncertainty of a given performance metric is affected by both model uncertainty and the finiteness of the validation sample (validation uncertainty). For a given performance metric, we show that the total uncertainty of the performance estimate can be decomposed into the uncertainty due to the model and the uncertainty due to the validation. Also, we propose $M^2$, the fraction of the total variance due to model uncertainty, and $V^2$, the fraction of the total variance due to validation uncertainty. These measures serve as complementary scalar indices that can be implemented for common performance metrics and visualizations such as calibration plots using simple Monte Carlo algorithms. Critically, our case study shows that with the same model and the same validation sample, the contribution of uncertainty sources is highly variable across performance metrics ($M^2$ varying from 12% for the Brier score to 78% for the calibration slope). This indicates that stakeholders who prioritize different aspects of performance (e.g., calibration versus clinical utility) might arrive at different decisions on whether future efforts should be directed towards creating a more reliable model or procuring a larger validation sample. In conclusion, external validation studies can readily be amended to incorporate model uncertainty, and we recommend that such studies report total variance as well as the relative share of variance components for all performance metrics.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Sadatsafavi, Paul Gustafson, Richard D. Riley

item.title: Data integration using propensity score weighting under missing at random
item.description: arXiv:2611.03353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study data integration for the setting in which a probability sample and a nonprobability sample are both available from a common target population, with auxiliary variables observed in both samples and the study variable observed only in the nonprobability sample. Under a parametric propensity score model for the nonprobability sample inclusion mechanism, we develop a conditional maximum likelihood estimator of the inclusion probabilities and construct an inverse probability weighted (IPW) estimator of the population mean. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed IPW estimator under suitable regularity conditions. To guard against misspecification of the propensity score model, we further incorporate an outcome regression model through debiased generalized entropy calibration (GEC) yielding a doubly robust estimator that remains consistent when the propensity score model or the outcome regression model is correctly specified. We also develop variance estimation procedures for both estimators. Simulation studies illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods, and we apply them to data from the Culture and Community in a Time of Crisis survey, where the nonprobability sample substantially over-represents certain demographic groups relative to the U.S.\ adult population.
item.dc:creator: Caleb Leedy, Jae Kwang Kim

item.title: Robustness against lying of the confidence interval for a fraction of population with a sensitive characteristic
item.description: arXiv:2611.03481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the investigations devoted to sensitive questions the problem is with the truthfulness of survey participants. We offer a fresh perspective on respondent deception. We investigate the influence of lying on the properties of the confidence intervals for the fraction of the sensitive part of a population. It is shown that the coverage probability is robust against lying.
item.dc:creator: Wojciech Zieli\'{n}ski

item.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series
item.description: arXiv:2611.03531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.
item.dc:creator: Gell\'ert Per\'enyi, Marco Piccininni, Mats J. Stensrud

item.title: Penalized Cox Regression with Graph-Structured Distribution-Valued Predictors
item.description: arXiv:2611.03608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose the Graph-Fused Distributional Cox Model (GFDCM), a penalized survival analysis framework for distribution-valued predictors organized on a known graph. Modern neuroimaging studies collect high-dimensional voxel-level measurements across multiple regions of interest (ROIs) with rich spatial dependency structures. Rather than reducing these to scalar summaries, GFDCM models the full distribution of voxel intensities within each ROI, retaining region-specific interpretability while exploiting spatial relationships among adjacent ROIs. The distributional associations are modeled using penalized splines. To achieve simultaneous predictor selection and graph-based fusion, we introduce a structured Graph-Fused Group LASSO (GFGL) penalty that combines a group-sparsity term for discarding irrelevant predictors with a fusion term that enforces coefficient functions for graph-adjacent predictors to be identical. A flexible alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm is employed to optimize the penalized partial likelihood. Numerical simulations illustrate satisfactory selection, fusion, and estimation performance of GFDCM compared with unpenalized functional Cox regression and selection-only alternatives. Finally, we apply GFDCM to baseline T1-weighted MRI data collected from 308 patients in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI-1) to identify brain regions associated with AD conversion. The results provide clinically meaningful insights and exhibit superior predictive performance compared to traditional ROI-level summary-based approaches.
item.dc:creator: Rahul Ghosal, Dhrubajyoti Ghosh, Yuanzhen Yue, Arkaprava Roy

item.title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.00266v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.
item.dc:creator: Felix Schur, Linus K\"uhne, Julius von K\"ugelgen, Jonas Peters

item.title: Pricing Today, Shaping Tomorrow: Contextual Dynamic Pricing in Purchase-Driven Evolving Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.00719v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Across diverse markets, it is important for firms to balance attracting customers with managing operational conditions, such as workloads and delivery times. Dynamic pricing plays a central role in this tradeoff, as the orders generated today can change the conditions faced by future customers. We develop a novel framework for contextual dynamic pricing with an observed shared state and unknown purchase-driven transitions. The valuation model allows unknown mean functions of customer covariates and state, unknown state-specific scales and a common unknown standardized noise distribution. We propose Shadow-Adjusted Pricing in Evolving Systems (SHAPE), which incorporates a purchase's future revenue consequences into current pricing. Purchase-shadow adjustment and scale standardization reveal a common one-dimensional oracle price map across states, allowing SHAPE to retain its pricing history across value updates without repeating coarse exploration. The same active sales records support price-map learning and joint updates of continuation values and purchase shadows, without fitting the noise distribution or full transition matrices. To support this reuse under purchase-driven feedback, we establish pricing guarantees for history-dependent inputs and stability bounds for the joint updates. Under regularity, coverage and design conditions, we obtain sublinear expected regret against a finite-horizon dynamic oracle for linear, H\"older and sparse linear mean models. For affine valuations at fixed state and feature dimensions, SHAPE matches the static semiparametric minimax time exponent up to logarithmic factors for every fixed noise-tail smoothness order $\beta\ge2$. Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appealing performance of SHAPE.
item.dc:creator: Jinjiang Zou, Yang Li, Zemin Zheng

item.title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
item.description: arXiv:2611.00979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.
item.dc:creator: Gengyu Xue, Fan Wang, Feiyu Jiang, Zifeng Zhao, Yi Yu

item.title: Unlikely likelihoods: likelihood analysis for the triangular and random histogram models
item.description: arXiv:2611.01030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper concerns certain parametric models for densities on the unit interval which lead to nonsmooth and nonregular likelihood functions. (i) The first is the simple triangular model on the unit interval, characterised by a density linearly increasing from zero to the mode position $\theta$ and then linearly decreasing to zero from the mode to one. With data from this model the likelihood function is a sum of individually log-convex terms, and with the derivative having discontinuities at each data point. (ii) The second is the one-parameter two-box density which is flat on $[0,\theta]$ and $(\theta,1]$, with $\theta$ the median. The likelihood has jumps at each datapoint. Here the maximum likelihood estimator is sharper than usual, with convergence in distribution of $n(\hat\theta-\theta)$ to a nonnormal limit. We also study the $k$-box extension of this model, with density being flat on $k$ boxes determined by $k$ quantiles. (iii) This second model is extended to the two-parameter two-box model, with areas $\gamma$ and $1-\gamma$ for boxes $[0,\theta]$ and $(\theta,1]$. Again the likelihood is nonregular, and the maximum likelihood estimators exhibit different rates of convergence for the breakpoints and the density values. The model generalises to the $2(k-1)$ parameter density piecewise flat over $k$ boxes. For each of these models we tend to the delicate task of sorting out the large-sample behaviour of the log-likelihoods, then leading to precise and partly nonstandard limit distributions for the maximum likelihood and Bayes estimators.
item.dc:creator: Nils Lid Hjort

item.title: Optimal Certified Multiple Testing with E-values
item.description: arXiv:2611.01333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study randomized multiple testing with e-values under arbitrary dependence and introduce a conditional certification constraint: Given the observed evidence, each coordinate's expected rejection certificate must not exceed its e-value. Existing randomized e-BH improvements satisfy this constraint but have no established optimality guarantee. We prove that the maximum conditional inclusion probability for hypothesis $i$, given e-values~$x$, is $1 \wedge (\alpha / K) \sum_j \min(x_i, x_j)$, and construct one rule attaining these bounds simultaneously. The rule uses a single independent uniform variable, rejects a prefix of the ordered e-values, and has a unique conditional rejection-set law among rules attaining all the bounds. It therefore maximizes every nonnegative weighted sum of inclusion probabilities, including expected true discoveries under any truth configuration. Under a shared uniform draw, its rejection set contains those of e-BH and U-eBH. The construction extends to BY-calibrated p-values, and simulations under positive and negative dependence show power gains over existing randomized procedures.
item.dc:creator: Soumyabrata Bose, Jay Bartroff

item.title: Principled Human-AI Collaboration in Agentic Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2611.01566v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Organizations adopting AI face the challenge of deciding which outputs can be released without human review while meeting the quality standards of human experts. We develop a statistical framework for delegating tasks between experts and black-box generate-verify workflows, in which AI-generated answers are verified and revised over multiple rounds. Before deployment, human experts evaluate selected outputs, and their judgments are used to calibrate the verifier threshold and number of attempts. Our method selects the policy with the highest estimated automation rate among statistically approved candidates, without modifying the generator or verifier. We establish finite-sample control of the error rate among released outputs, characterize the expert evaluations sufficient to attain a target automation rate, and derive a minimax lower bound establishing rate optimality in the quality margin and required confidence. In a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, average held-out automation increases from 2.50% to 24.17% as expert evaluations accumulate, while released-output error rates remain around 1.20%. In contrast, heuristics that release answers after consistently high verifier scores either violate the 5% error tolerance or automate at most 1.30% of tasks. Synthetic experiments further examine these theoretical predictions under controlled settings.
item.dc:creator: Young Hyun Cho, Will Wei Sun

item.title: Moment-Orthogonal Quadratic-Envelope E-Processes for Anytime-Valid Location Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.01637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: E-process confidence sequences for unbounded means typically use a variance bound and a first-order score, leaving skewness and kurtosis unused. We construct a quadratic-envelope e-process from a conditionally centered vector score with a predictable second-moment bound. Under moment information specified independently of the tested stream, it stays positive on unbounded support and gives exact anytime-valid coverage under predictable strategies and fixed mixtures, without score clipping. For a location family with known central moments through order four, the centered observation and its centered square yield an exact confidence sequence whose local width shrinks, relative to a first-order construction, by a factor determined by skewness and kurtosis. At level 5%, the largest null ever-crossing rate was 4.63%; on two zero-inflated-lognormal families median stopping times fell by 36.8-45.8%. When the moments are calibrated on an independent reference sample, a centering-robust factor keeps exact coverage at a closed-form width cost: the median gain was 21.6-30.3% for Gamma(2) and lognormal errors with 10^6 reference observations, and a loss of up to 9.9% with 10^4. On public Fermi gamma-ray detector data with a declared stability margin, it crossed at the current location in 1.8% of 225 windows and stopped 30-35% earlier than the calibrated first-order method.
item.dc:creator: Serhii Zabolotnii

item.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
item.description: arXiv:2611.01666v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
item.dc:creator: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen

item.title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units
item.description: arXiv:2611.01854v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article shows how researchers can exploit \textit{locally exogeneous variation} even in the presence of endogeneity, autocorrelation, or spurious correlation. It describes the infill asymptotic properties of generalized least squares estimation with county-level data, Census tract-level data, and similar regional averages, including sufficient conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid inference.
item.dc:creator: Christopher W. Engh

item.title: Randomized Adaptive Sequential Allocation and the Limits of Bounded Exposure to Inferior Treatments
item.description: arXiv:2611.02012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A clinical trial must learn which treatment is superior while sparing its participants from the inferior one. Kundu et al. 2025 recently showed that a purely deterministic rule, which always assigns the treatment with the larger current sample mean, achieves a strong form of this ethical goal. The smaller allocation count stays almost surely finite and has all moments bounded uniformly in the sample size. Deterministic allocation is, however, predictable, and predictability invites selection bias. We ask whether this bounded-exposure phenomenon survives once the deterministic rule is replaced by a smooth randomized one. We show that it does not. Under any fixed non-degenerate symmetric randomization, both treatments are sampled infinitely often, the adaptive sample means are strongly consistent, and the inferior treatment draws a strictly positive limiting allocation proportion. Consequently, the inferior allocation count grows linearly and its moments are unbounded. We then study annealed randomization, in which the randomization scale cools with the accumulated information, and obtain summability and divergence criteria that separate finite, sublinear, and linear exposure. A forced-exploration variant identifies the superior treatment with probability one while keeping the inferior exposure sublinear, and thereby frees the annealed guarantees from any correct-stabilization event. We also treat normalized multi-treatment rules, ties, indifference zones, unequal variances, general response distributions, and local alternatives. Finally, we develop the post-trial asymptotic inference that each exposure regime permits. The results delineate the trade-off between allocation concealment, persistent exploration, and ethical concentration on the superior treatment.
item.dc:creator: Sampurna Kundu, Monitirtha Dey, Atanu Biswas

item.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
item.description: arXiv:2611.02029v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.
item.dc:creator: Jiuyi Cheng, Alexis Akira Toda

item.title: A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines
item.description: arXiv:2611.02413v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: MRI morphometry pipelines are often evaluated by measurement agreement or downstream accuracy, yet their scientific value depends on the conclusions they support. Two pipelines can produce similar feature-level results yet support different conclusions about aging, cognitive decline, or neurodegeneration. We introduce Scientific Claim Stability (SCS), a claim-centric evaluation framework that converts region-of-interest (ROI) morphometry tables into auditable claim cards and evaluates their support under changes in dataset, processing pipeline, atlas, feature family, and target. Across 10,370 MRI scans from three datasets and five cohorts, SCS generates 2,783 claim cards and evaluates 89 claim-family pairs. The evaluation distinguishes stable, transferable, and fragile claims. FreeSurfer 8-FastSurfer comparisons show high evidence concordance and low anatomical-support overlap under the primary covariate specification. Acquisition-adjusted analyses show that the magnitude of support disagreement depends on the model specification. Structured review by specialists in geriatrics, neuroscience, and radiology, alongside auxiliary ChatGPT and Gemini reviewers, assesses claim plausibility, clarity, faithfulness, usefulness, and caution. SCS provides a reproducible way to audit the evidential stability of morphometry claims without assuming a universal gold standard.
item.dc:creator: Duy-Cat Can, Dang-Duat Tran, Anh-Khang Nguyen, Quoc-Bao Tran, Trung-Hieu Do, Van-Tu Nguyen, Duy-Thanh Vu, Oliver Y. Ch\'en, Hoang-Quynh Le

item.title: Diagnosing Model--Item Interactions in Language Model Benchmarks with LSIRM
item.description: arXiv:2611.02432v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models with similar benchmark accuracy can succeed on different items. Overall scores do not show where their performance differs or which item properties might explain those differences. We demonstrate how the latent space item response model (LSIRM) can help evaluators investigate these patterns and their consequences for model comparison. We analyze 1,348 language models on 5,761 BBH items and compare ways of presenting and scoring answers across BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MuSR. We examine LSIRM maps, which summarize differences in performance across models and items, alongside item properties and records of correct and incorrect responses. In BBH, nearby items on these maps often share the same correct answer, such as "Yes" or "No." Across the four benchmarks, this pattern is stronger when answers are scored using option labels, such as A, B, C, and D, than when using the text of the options. We then estimate each model's tendency to perform better or worse on items with particular correct answers and quantify how this tendency contributes to its score. This separates an estimated contribution associated with correct answers from the remaining differences in item performance. Two models' total numbers of correct answers differed by only 14 out of 5,761 items. Excluding the estimated answer-category contribution from their scores moved their ranks hundreds of places in opposite directions, while keeping all other estimates unchanged. The approach helps evaluators identify differences hidden by overall accuracy and understand how the choice of what to include in a score affects model rankings.
item.dc:creator: Jinwen Luo, Han Jiang, Ziang Xiao, Susu Zhang

item.title: Selective Randomization Inference for Interference
item.description: arXiv:2611.02443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Empirical researchers often use tests for interference as pretests or robustness checks. However, when the results guide the choice of models, parameters, or hypotheses, the resulting data-dependent selection can compromise the validity of subsequent inference. This paper develops a two-stage selective randomization inference framework for interference that explicitly conditions on the selection event to account for data-dependent selection. We first test the null hypothesis of no treatment spillover using a conditional randomization method. If this null is rejected, we test the null hypothesis of zero exposure contrast under a pre-specified exposure mapping that allows for spillover effects; otherwise, we test the null hypothesis of no direct effects under the assumption of no spillover. We prove that each second-stage test controls the selective Type I error rate in finite samples and evaluate the size and power of the proposed tests through Monte Carlo experiments.
item.dc:creator: Takahide Yanagi

item.title: Exact Simes inequalities for two-sided Gaussian tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.02513v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Simes test combines marginal p-values to test a global null hypothesis. Whether it controls the type I error for two-sided Gaussian tests with arbitrary covariance remains open. We prove that, for every fixed number $m$ of tests, the rejection probability does not exceed the nominal level when that level is sufficiently small. The same range of levels works for every covariance matrix. Equality holds if and only if the p-values form independent groups with identical values within each group. For $m=3$, a computer-assisted proof establishes validity at $0.05$, and an analytic argument extends it to an explicit interval around $0.05$. As the number $m$ of tests increases, we prove validity in two settings: each test statistic is correlated with at most a fixed number of others; or the statistics form independent blocks whose sizes grow sufficiently slowly, at a specified rate of order $\log\log m$. Both settings allow arbitrary correlations within these restrictions. For any fixed $0<a<1$, validity holds for every $m$ above a threshold $M$ and every level $0<\alpha\le a$; the same $M$ works for all allowed covariances. Further results quantify the difference between the nominal level and the rejection probability, and permit more correlated neighbors when their correlations are bounded away from $\pm1$. We do not obtain numerical values for the general small-level cutoffs or the required number of tests.
item.dc:creator: Xianyang Zhang

item.title: Where Is a Prediction Model Miscalibrated, and for Whom? Local Audits in Outcome-Learned Pockets
item.description: arXiv:2611.02639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Overall and group-level averages, and ranking metrics such as the AUC, can hide sets of observations for which a prediction model systematically over- or under-predicts. We present an audit that asks where a model is miscalibrated (in which sets of similar observations it over- or under-predicts on average) and for whom (whether its average prediction error differs between demographic groups, such as by race or sex, within the same set). It groups observations into pockets using random-forest similarity, which weighs each feature by its importance for predicting the outcome, with a ridge-regression grouping alongside. Pockets are learned on one sample and tested on another, with simultaneous confidence intervals that allow for correlation within units such as hospitals; the audit needs only features, outcomes and fixed predictions. In 17 simulation scenarios with an error planted for one group, the combined audit located it better than the strongest alternative grouping in 15, with false-alarm rates near or below 5%; with a local error planted for everyone, it won in 12 of 15 scenarios at the smaller error size and lost when the error was unrelated to the outcome. In public synthetic data from the care-management algorithm studied by Obermeyer et al., it found no detectable overall error but under-prediction of illness in the sickest pockets and over-prediction elsewhere, and distinguished Black patients' concentration where the score under-predicted for everyone from a Black-White gap within pockets. For APACHE IVa, an exploratory analysis located its previously reported over-prediction of ICU mortality in a mostly ventilated pocket and a low-risk pocket, with none detected in a moderate-risk one. Two chest X-ray classifiers showed offsetting local errors behind no detectable overall error. Code: https://github.com/modenesi/pocket-audit
item.dc:creator: Bernardo Modenesi, Taoyi Chen, Sima Najafzadehkhoei, Lucia Wang, Ameya Diwan, Beatrice Knudsen

item.title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards
item.description: arXiv:2611.03166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.
item.dc:creator: Harald Kugler, Leonard Henckel, Sebastian Weichwald

item.title: Specification LASSO and a Flexible Characteristics-Based Asset Pricing Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.03391v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies a partially linear semiparametric additive model that allows for interactions among variables in high-dimensional settings. We propose the Specification LASSO (S-LASSO), a two-step method that integrates LASSO and Adaptive Group LASSO to simultaneously perform variable selection and model specification. Theoretically, we establish that S-LASSO possesses oracle properties in terms of selection consistency and asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that S-LASSO outperforms existing alternatives across a variety of scenarios. Empirically, we apply S-LASSO to a characteristics-based asset pricing model, exploring the linear and nonlinear effects of asset-specific characteristics on cross-sectional returns, as well as their interactions with firm size.
item.dc:creator: Chaohua Dong, Shuyi Ge, Shaoran Li, Wen Su

item.title: Fast nonparametric estimation of sparse precision matrices with a priori sparsity structure
item.description: arXiv:2611.03462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work describes a computational approach for rapidly estimating and characterizing the covariance structure of a Gaussian random field from a modest number of i.i.d. replicates by formulating the problem in terms of a sparse inverse Cholesky factor of the data's covariance matrix. Borrowing from the extensive literature of using directed acyclic graphs to impose sparsity on inverse Cholesky factors (for example, Vecchia's approximation or nearest-neighbor Gaussian process models), a probabilistically parsimonious a priori sparsity pattern is imposed, and with careful formulation the estimation problem is given as an extremely well-structured convex problem that can be solved for millions of unknowns in seconds on a single processor core. After describing the problem and specific formulation of the optimization, we demonstrate the estimator's speed and effectiveness at capturing a variety of nonstationary structures in spatial or spatio-temporal data, and in ensemble data assimilation.
item.dc:creator: Caleb Derrickson, Alexis Montoison, Vishwas Rao, Christopher J. Geoga, Mihai Anitescu

item.title: Unconfoundedness as an Information Constraint
item.description: arXiv:2611.03550v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper provides an information-theoretic characterization of unconfoundedness within a general class of models allowing for endogenous selection. We impose a conditional mutual information (CMI) restriction requiring that the information about treatment contained in a potential outcome, conditional on covariates, does not exceed that contained in its latent heterogeneity. Under the maintained model conditions, this restriction is equivalent to a multiplicative factorization of treatment probabilities into separate functions of latent heterogeneity and covariates. Although the CMI restriction permits endogenous selection, sufficiently rich variation in treatment probabilities across covariate values makes it equivalent to unconfoundedness for the corresponding potential outcome. For binary treatments, any nonconstant propensity score suffices; for multiple treatments, a full-rank condition on the second-moment matrix of the propensity-score vector is sufficient. State-specific restrictions bound residual selection and imply exogeneity for individual treatment states under boundary-support conditions. Extensions cover continuous treatments and instrument exogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Breunig

item.title: Studentized inference in randomized experiments when a few units dominate the outcome variation
item.description: arXiv:2611.03561v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In completely randomized experiments with heavy-tailed outcomes, a few units can carry a share of the residual variation that does not vanish as the number of units grows. We study the studentized difference in means and Lin's regression-adjusted estimator, with covariates whose leverage vanishes, when the finite population is fixed, and the treatment assignment is the only source of randomness. The studentized statistic then has a nonnormal limit in general. Populations with the same marginal distributions of potential outcomes can have different limits, as the limit depends on the unobserved pairing mechanism of the two potential outcomes of each dominant unit. When the outcome errors are drawn from a heavy-tailed law, the limit is random and, outside a degenerate case, varies with the population. Under balanced allocation, the conventional Wald interval has an explicit asymptotic coverage floor. At the nominal level $0.95$, the floor is about $0.42$ for every population and about $0.84$ when the two potential residuals of each unit are equal. Both floors are close to the best possible, and without balanced allocation, the coverage can fall to the smaller of the proportions of treated and control units.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Chen, Jonathan W. Kiesel, Jonathan R. Woody

item.title: Benchmark Prediction with Sparse and Unpaired Cached Responses
item.description: arXiv:2611.03614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating a generative model on all queries from all available benchmark tasks is prohibitively expensive. As such, models are often evaluated on different subsets of tasks and/or different subsets of queries from a given task. The resulting collection of responses and the corresponding (model, task) score matrix are sparse and unpaired. In this paper, we introduce the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a collection of low-dimensional representations of models based on their embedded responses. PKPS generalizes existing methods for representing black-box generative models by comparing responses to similar -- rather than just identical -- queries and is therefore able to utilize sparse and unpaired information. Theoretically, we show that benchmark prediction using PKPS is query-efficient relative to methods that only use information from dense and paired portions of the evaluation data. Empirically, we show that PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.
item.dc:creator: Hayden Helm, Avijit Ghosh, Ben Johnson, Carey Priebe

item.title: Multiwinner Elections and the Spoiler Effect
item.description: arXiv:2403.03228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the popular debate over the use of ranked-choice voting, it is often claimed that the method of single transferable vote (STV) is immune or mostly immune to the so-called ``spoiler effect,'' where the removal of a losing candidate changes the set of winners. This claim has previously been studied only in the single-winner case. We investigate how susceptible STV is to the spoiler effect in multiwinner elections, where the output of the voting method is a committee of size at least two. To evaluate STV we compare it to numerous other voting methods including single non-transferable vote, $k$-Borda, and the Chamberlin-Courant rule. We provide simulation results under three different random models and empirical results using a large database of real-world multiwinner political elections from Scotland. Our results show that STV is not spoiler-proof in any meaningful sense in the multiwinner context, but it tends to perform well relative to other methods, especially when using real-world ballot data.
item.dc:creator: Brian Brubach, Matthew I. Jones, David McCune, Jennifer Wilson

item.title: Stage-wise semiparametric analysis of multivariate event times under informative censoring via vine copula
item.description: arXiv:2502.20608v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The analysis of times to multiple nonterminal events arises in many lifetime data settings, where the nonterminal event times are subject to informative censoring by a terminal event, posing substantial challenges. We propose a likelihood-based regression framework that models dependence among multiple nonterminal and terminal event times using a vine copula. This framework allows pairwise associations between nonterminal and terminal events, as well as among nonterminal events, to vary across event types, while enabling valid regression inference for the marginal distributions of individual event times. To facilitate computation, we develop a stage-wise pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure and establish its large-sample properties. We demonstrate satisfactory finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators and associated variance estimators through simulation studies. We also illustrate the proposed methodology using data from a crowdfunding platform to examine the relationship between different types of creator-backer interactions and a creator's lifetime on the platform.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Chen, Yiwei Li, Qian M. Zhou

item.title: A Generalized Tangent Approximation based Variational Inference Framework for Strongly Super-Gaussian Likelihoods
item.description: arXiv:2504.05431v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Variational inference, as an alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, has played a transformative role in enabling scalable computation for complex Bayesian models. Nevertheless, existing approaches often depend on either rigid model-specific formulations or stochastic black-box optimization routines. Tangent approximation is a principled class of structured variational methods that exploit the geometry of the underlying probability model. However, its utility has largely been confined to logistic regression and related modeling regimes. In this article, we propose a novel variational framework based on tangent transformation for a broad class of probability models characterized by strongly super-Gaussian likelihoods. Our method leverages convex duality to construct tangent minorants of the log-likelihood, thereby inducing conjugacy with Gaussian priors over model parameters in an otherwise intractable setup. Under mild assumptions on the data-generating mechanism, we establish algorithmic convergence guarantees, a contribution that stands in contrast to the limited theoretical assurances typically available for black-box variational methods. Additionally, we derive near-parametric variational risk bounds. Superior performance of our proposed methodology is illustrated on simulated and real-data scenarios that challenge state-of-the-art variational algorithms in terms of scalability and their ability to consistently capture complex underlying data structure.
item.dc:creator: Somjit Roy, Pritam Dey, Debdeep Pati, Bani K. Mallick

item.title: Model-based inference in complex surveys through targeted resampling of weights
item.description: arXiv:2504.11636v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Survey data often arises from complex sampling designs, such as stratified or multistage sampling, with unequal inclusion probabilities. When sampling is informative, traditional inference methods yield biased estimators and poor coverage. Classical pseudo-likelihood-based methods provide accurate asymptotic inference but lack finite-sample uncertainty quantification and the ability to integrate prior information. Existing Bayesian approaches, like the Bayesian pseudo-posterior estimator and weighted finite population Bayesian bootstrap, have limitations; the former struggles with uncertainty quantification, while the latter is computationally intensive and sensitive to bootstrap replicates. We propose the Survey-adjusted Weighted Likelihood Bootstrap (S-WLB), a computationally efficient framework that accounts for informative sampling by resampling random weights from a carefully chosen distribution centered around the underlying sampling weights. We establish conditional consistency and asymptotic normality of the S-WLB, showing that its uncertainty intervals are asymptotically valid. We further develop the Survey-adjusted Posterior Bootstrap (S-PB), which extends S-WLB to incorporate prior information. Using an Edgeworth expansion, we characterize the second-order influence of the prior on S-PB while retaining the first-order asymptotic properties inherited from S-WLB. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed methods through simulations and applications to nationally representative survey datasets like NHANES and NSDUH.
item.dc:creator: Snigdha Das, Dipankar Bandyopadhyay, Debdeep Pati

item.title: Robust normality transformation and outlier detection in diverse distributions, with application to functional neuroimaging data
item.description: arXiv:2505.11806v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Normality transformations improve conformity with parametric assumptions and, for outlier detection, facilitate parametric thresholds. However, transformation parameters must be estimated from data that may contain contamination, which can distort the transformation of non-outlying observations and lead to masking and swamping. Recently developed robust power transformations address skew but not more general departures from normality, and they remain vulnerable to outliers due to reliance on Huber M-estimators of location and scale, which are heavily biased under contamination. Here, we propose a novel robust transformation based on the flexible sinh--arcsinh (SHASH) family of distributions, which accommodates skewness, non-Gaussian tail weights, and combinations thereof. To robustly estimate the transformation, we consider two methods for initializing outliers: a conventional distance-based approach and a novel variant of anomaly detection. Through extensive simulations and real data analyses, we find that robust SHASH transformation more successfully transforms non-outlying observations toward normality and better identifies outliers at contamination levels up to 20%, compared with existing approaches. In an application to fMRI volume censoring using robust MCD distances, which are approximately $F$-distributed under Gaussianity, robust normality transformation improves distinction of artifactual volumes, illustrating its potential as a preprocessing step for automatic, robust multivariate outlier detection in large neuroimaging studies.
item.dc:creator: Fatma Parlak, Saranjeet Singh Saluja, Amanda Mejia

item.title: Quantifying structural uncertainty in chemical reaction network inference
item.description: arXiv:2505.15653v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamical systems in biology are complex, and one often does not have comprehensive knowledge about the interactions involved. Chemical reaction network (CRN) inference aims to identify, from observing species concentrations over time, the unknown reactions between the species. Existing approaches such as sparse regularisation largely focus on identifying a single, most likely CRN, without addressing uncertainty about the network structure. However, it is important to quantify structural uncertainty to have confidence in our inference and predictions. In this work, we explore how effective sparse regularisation methods are for quantifying structural uncertainty. Locally optimal solutions to sparse regularisation are mapped to CRN structures; however, it is unclear whether this approach encompasses all plausible CRNs. We find that inducing sparsity with nonconvex penalty functions results in better coverage of the plausible CRNs compared to the popular lasso regularisation. To validate our approach, we apply our methods to real-world data examples, and are able to simultaneously recover reactions proposed across multiple literature sources for a reaction system. Our emphasis on network-level probabilities enables a novel, hierarchical representation of structural ambiguities in the space of CRNs. This representation translates into alternative reaction pathways suggested by the available data, thus guiding the efforts of future experimental design.
item.dc:creator: Yong See Foo, Adriana Zanca, Jennifer A. Flegg, Ivo Siekmann

item.title: Exact, Nonparametric Sensitivity Analysis for Observational Studies of Contingency Tables
item.description: arXiv:2507.17207v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In observational studies, contingency tables are commonly used to examine associations between categorical variables. However, any test of association in contingency tables may be biased by unmeasured confounding, and existing sensitivity analyses typically assume a binary treatment or impose strong parametric assumptions on non-binary treatments. We develop an exact (non-asymptotic) and nonparametric sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in $I \times J$ and $I\times J\times K$ contingency tables, accommodating both non-binary treatments and outcomes. Extending Rosenbaum's generic bias sensitivity model, we derive a general method to compute the exact worst-case null distribution for any count-based test, including chi-squared and likelihood-based tests of association. We further provide specialized results for subfamilies of count-based tests that enable more efficient computation of the worst-case null distribution. Finally, we investigate test power in sensitivity analyses and show that tests exploiting all treatment and outcome levels achieve higher power than tests that dichotomize the categorical variables. We illustrate the proposed methods with a re-analysis of the effect of pre-kindergarten care on math achievement using data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study. The R package sensitivityIxJ that implements the method is on CRAN.
item.dc:creator: Elaine K. Chiu, Hyunseung Kang

item.title: Model-Free Machine Learning and Inference in High-Dimensional Binary Classification via Repro Samples
item.description: arXiv:2510.01468v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a model-free yet interpretable machine learning and inference approach for binary classification of high-dimensional data from an unstructured model by leveraging a class of (likely misspecified) working sparse generalized linear models (GLMs). Our method builds on the repro samples framework, which utilizes artificial samples that mimic the true data and noise for inference. Our inference targets both the model support and regression coefficients of the oracle model, defined as the working GLM closest to the unknown true model. The development offers several advantages: (1) it is model-free, requiring neither specific model assumptions, nor sparsity of the true model; (2) for model support, it constructs a model candidate set for the most influential covariates with guaranteed coverage under a weak signal condition; (3) for oracle coefficients, it provides confidence sets for any linear transformations of the coefficients. When the oracle model coincides with the true model, the inference results apply to the true model, allowing simultaneous quantification of uncertainty in (discrete) model selection and (continuous) parameter estimation. It provides an interpretable machine learning approach otherwise not possible when using a black-box model. Simulations and an application to RNA-seq immune response data are used to illustrate the method's performance.
item.dc:creator: Xiaotian Hou, Peng Wang, Minge Xie, Linjun Zhang

item.title: Sequentially Doubly Robust Estimation of Conditional Survival Probability with Time-Varying Covariates
item.description: arXiv:2510.10372v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is often of interest to study the association between covariates and the cumulative incidence of a right-censored time-to-event outcome. When time-varying covariates are measured on a fixed discrete time scale, it is desirable to account for more up-to-date covariates that may inform future censoring. Existing methods rely on stringent parametric assumptions, do not account for informative censoring due to time-varying covariates for continuous time, estimate a marginal survival probability, or do not fully use the discrete-time structure of time-varying covariates. We propose a nonparametric and sequentially doubly robust estimator of the continuous-time survival probability conditional on covariates in this setting. We also show that, in the special case of estimating the marginal survival probability, our estimator is asymptotically efficient. We demonstrate the superior performance of our estimator in a simulation experiment, and apply the method to a COVID-19 vaccine efficacy trial.
item.dc:creator: Hongxiang Qiu, Marco Carone, Alex Luedtke, Peter B. Gilbert

item.title: PLS-SEM-power: A Shiny App and R package for Computing Required Sample Size and Minimum Detectable Effect Size in PLS-SEMs
item.description: arXiv:2511.14546v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite its evanescent nature, statistical power is crucial for planning Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) studies. This brief paper introduces PLS-SEM-power, a Shiny Application and R package that implements the inverse square root method by Kock and Hadaya (2018) to calculate both the minimum required sample size (a priori analysis) and the Minimum Detectable Effect Size (MDES, sensitivity analysis), given a chosen significance level (alpha level) and desired statistical power (1 - beta), set to 0.80 by default. The software supports both one-tailed and two-tailed calculations, with one-tailed calculations as the default following the formulation of Kock and Hadaya (2018), and provides an intuitive user interface, facilitating reproducible and easily accessible analyses in diverse research contexts.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Ansani

item.title: Correlation Matters! Streamlining the Sample Size Procedure with Hierarchical Time-to-event Endpoints
item.description: arXiv:2511.16773v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Composite endpoints are widely used in cardiovascular clinical trials to improve statistical efficiency while preserving clinical relevance. The win ratio (WR) measure and more general frameworks of win statistics have emerged as popular alternatives to traditional time-to-first-event analyses. Although analytic sample size formulas for WR have been developed, they rely on design parameters that are often not straightforward to specify. Consequently, sample size determination in clinical trials with WR for the primary analysis is most often based on simulations, which, however, can be computationally intensive. To address this challenge, we derive refined formulas to calculate the proportions of wins, losses, and ties for multiple prioritized time-to-event endpoints to assist with study planning. These formulas rely on familiar design inputs and become directly applicable when integrated with existing sample size methods. We conduct a comprehensive assessment of how correlation among endpoints affects sample size requirements across varying design features, and demonstrate the role of correlations through case studies to generate further insights.
item.dc:creator: Yunhan Mou, Fan Li, Denise Esserman, Yuan Huang

item.title: High-dimensional Autoregressive Modeling for Time Series with Hierarchical Structures
item.description: arXiv:2512.00508v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-dimensional data, especially time-dependent data with increasingly complex structures, have become ubiquitous in modern applications, and hierarchical relationships among variables are increasingly common. However, there is still a lack of supervised learning tools in the literature for them. To fill this gap, we introduce a new model-designing framework, and it then combines with unsupervised factor modeling tools to form an efficient and interpretable autoregressive model for high-dimensional time series with hierarchical structures. An ordinary least squares estimation is considered, and its non-asymptotic properties are established. Moreover, we propose an algorithm to search for estimates, and a boosting method is also suggested for hyperparameter selection. Simulation experiments are conducted to evaluate finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology, and its usefulness is demonstrated by an application to the Personality-120 dataset.
item.dc:creator: Lan Li, Shibo Yu, Yingzhou Wang, Guodong Li

item.title: Causal Inference and Evidence Synthesis for Semi-continuous Exposures with Multiple Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2512.09237v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Semi-continuous exposure variables, featuring a point mass at zero and a continuous dose in exposed individuals, arise frequently in epidemiology. In such settings, investigators may wish to distinguish the causal effect of exposure at a fixed dose with no exposure, from the dose-response effect among exposed individuals. We develop a two-stage framework for causal inference with semi-continuous exposures and multiple outcomes. The proposed approach yields outcome-specific estimators for these two causal components, establishes their large sample properties, and provides Wald-type tests for homogeneity across outcomes. We further extend the framework to the multi-cohort setting through hierarchical homogeneity testing and evidence synthesis, enabling principled pooling across cohorts and outcomes. We apply the proposed methods to several cohort studies designed to evaluate the effects of prenatal alcohol exposure on executive function, mathematics achievement, and learning and memory. Simulation studies show that the proposed estimators and testing procedures perform well. The framework provides a principled basis for estimation, comparison, and synthesis of causal effects with multiple outcomes and semi-continuous exposures.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoya Wang, Richard J. Cook, Yeying Zhu, Tugba Akkaya-Hocagil, R. Colin Carter, Sandra W. Jacobson, Joseph L. Jacobson, Nancy Day, Louise M. Ryan

item.title: Measures and Models of Non-Monotonic Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2512.10828v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A margin-free measure of bivariate association generalizing Spearman's rho to the case of non-monotonic dependence is defined in terms of two square integrable functions on the unit interval. Properties of generalized Spearman correlation are investigated when the functions are piecewise continuous and strictly monotonic, with particular focus on the special cases where the functions are drawn from orthonormal bases defined by Legendre polynomials and cosine functions. For continuous random variables, generalized Spearman correlation is treated as a copula-based measure and shown to depend on a pair of uniform-distribution-preserving (udp) transformations determined by the underlying functions. Bounds for generalized Spearman correlation are derived and a novel technique referred to as stochastic inversion of udp transformations is used to construct singular copulas that attain the bounds and parametric copulas with densities that interpolate between the bounds and model different degrees of non-monotonic dependence. Sample analogues of generalized Spearman correlation are proposed and their asymptotic properties are investigated. Potential applications of the theory are demonstrated including: exploratory analyses of the dependence structures of datasets and their symmetries; elicitation of functions maximizing generalized Spearman correlation via expansions in orthonormal basis functions; and construction of tractable probability densities to model a wide variety of non-monotonic dependencies.
item.dc:creator: Alexander J. McNeil, Johanna G. Neslehova, Andrew D. Smith

item.title: Decoupled Kemeny quasi-likelihoods for rank-based generalised linear models
item.description: arXiv:2601.00188v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces a unified profile quasi-likelihood framework for generalised linear models built on a topologically complete extension to Kendall's $\tau$ with finite sample power and Type-I error rates. By establishing equivalence between continuous $L^2$ profile estimators and discrete Generalized Gibbs exponential families, we prove local asymptotic minimax efficiency over the copula tangent space. The framework yields monotone-affine invariant inference, sub-Gaussian concentration bounds, and exact finite-sample $t$-pivot tail majorization under arbitrary tie configurations. We illustrate the methodology through three canonical applications: bivariate rank correlation, paired testing, and intraclass correlation.
item.dc:creator: Landon Hurley

item.title: Finite-sample Valid Permutation Inference under Multi-way Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2601.08610v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Econometric applications with multi-way clustering often feature a small number of effective clusters or heavy-tailed data, making standard cluster-robust and bootstrap inference unreliable in finite samples. In this paper, we develop a framework for finite-sample valid permutation inference in linear regression with multi-way clustering under an assumption of conditional exchangeability of the errors. Our assumption is closely related to the notion of separate exchangeability studied in earlier work, but can be more realistic in many economic settings as it imposes minimal restrictions on the covariate distribution. We construct permutation tests of significance that are valid in finite samples and establish theoretical power guarantees, in contrast to existing methods that are justified only asymptotically. While our main presentation is under exchangeable errors, our framework encompasses invariance-based tests that remain valid under general forms of heteroskedastic errors. We also extend our methodology to settings with missing data and derive power results that reveal phase transitions in detectability. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that the proposed tests maintain correct size and competitive power, while standard cluster-robust and bootstrap procedures can exhibit substantial size distortions.
item.dc:creator: Wenxuan Guo, Panos Toulis, Yuhao Wang

item.title: Impact Range Assessment (IRA): An Interpretable Sensitivity Measure for Machine Learning Regression Modelling
item.description: arXiv:2602.05239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While machine learning regression models capture the relationship between predictors and the response variable, they often lack intuitive methods to help modelers understand how sensitive model predictions are to changes in individual predictors. To address this limitation, we introduce a model-agnostic interpretability method called Impact Range Assessment (IRA), which quantifies the sensitivity of model predictions to changes in each predictor by measuring the range of predicted responses as the predictor varies across its observed range. Validation using synthetic linear and nonlinear datasets demonstrates that relevant predictors produced higher IRA values than irrelevant ones. Moreover, repeated evaluations produced results aligned with those from the single-execution analysis, confirming the method's robustness. For demonstration, two benchmark datasets were used to evaluate IRA across five machine learning regression models, yielding model-specific sensitivity rankings and supporting IRA's applicability as a complementary sensitivity analysis tool alongside feature importance methods such as permutation feature importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).
item.dc:creator: Jihao You, Dan Tulpan, Jiaojiao Diao, Jennifer L. Ellis

item.title: Zero Variance Portfolio
item.description: arXiv:2602.19462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When the number of assets is larger than the sample size, the minimum variance portfolio interpolates the training data, delivering pathological zero in-sample variance. We show that if the weights of the zero variance portfolio are learned by a novel ``Ridgelet'' estimator, in a new test data this portfolio enjoys out-of-sample generalizability. It exhibits the double descent phenomenon and can achieve optimal risk in the overparametrized regime when the number of assets dominates the sample size. In contrast, a ``Ridgeless'' estimator which invokes the pseudoinverse fails in-sample interpolation and diverges away from out-of-sample optimality. Extensive simulations and empirical studies demonstrate that the Ridgelet method performs competitively in high-dimensional portfolio optimization.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Yi Ding, Zhentao Shi, Bo Zhang

item.title: Robust Regression with Student's T: The Role of Degrees of Freedom
item.description: arXiv:2603.00269v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linear regression estimators are known to be sensitive to outliers, and one alternative to obtain a robust and efficient estimator of the regression parameter is to model the error with Student's $t$ distribution. In this article, we compare estimators of the degrees of freedom parameter in the $t$ distribution using frequentist and Bayesian maximum a posteriori methods, and study properties of the corresponding estimated regression coefficients. We include a comparison with some recommended approaches in the literature, including fixing the degrees of freedom and robust regression using the Huber loss function. Our results suggest that estimating the degrees of freedom by maximizing the adjusted profile log-likelihood function often yields accurate estimates of the regression coefficients, with performance comparable to that obtained by fixing the degrees of freedom at their true values. These findings provide a detailed synthesis of $t$-based robust regression and underscore a key insight: the proper calibration of the degrees of freedom is as crucial as the choice of the robust distribution itself for achieving optimal performance. The R package that implements our method is available at https://github.com/amanda-ng518/RobustTRegression
item.dc:creator: Amanda Ng, Shangkai Zhu, Archer Gong Zhang, Nancy Reid

item.title: Time Partitioning in Target Trial Emulation
item.description: arXiv:2603.15924v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In target trial emulation, the treatment strategies that patients follow are inferred from the treatments they actually receive in routine care. However, in most settings, the outcome may preclude the observation of planned treatment, giving rise to immortal time bias through misclassification of treatment strategy, while markers of treatment response may influence subsequent treatment decisions, giving rise to time-varying confounding. A key step toward unbiased treatment effect estimation is to partition follow-up into sufficiently short time intervals to unfold the feedback relationships involving treatment and represent the resulting causal relations with a directed acyclic graph. In this study, we present the possible within-interval causal orderings induced by this partitioning, discuss their causal implications, and assess their plausibility across clinical settings. For each causal ordering, we derive the corresponding g-formula. Using ancestral multi-world networks and simulations, we show that the standard cloning-censoring-weighting estimator is invalid when treatment affects the outcome within a time interval, and we propose a modified version of the method that restores its validity in this setting. Finally, we analyze the consequences of choosing time intervals that are either excessively wide or excessively narrow, thereby formally establishing the need for time partitioning and providing practical guidance for selecting an appropriate partition based on the clinical setting.
item.dc:creator: Harold Tankpinou Zoumenou (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, F75012 Paris, France), Simon Ferreira (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, F75012 Paris, France), Charles Assaad (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, F75012 Paris, France), David Hajage (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, Equipe PEPITES, Assistance Publique - H\^opitaux de Paris, H\^opital Piti\'e Salp\^etri\`ere, D\'epartement de Sant\'e Publique, Centre de Pharmaco\'epid\'emiologie), Alexandra Beurton (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, UMRS 1158 Neurophysiologie Respiratoire Exp\'erimentale et Clinique, APHP, H\^opital Tenon, Department of Intensive Care, F75012 Paris, France), Fabrice Carrat (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, APHP, H\^opital Saint-Antoine, D\'epartement de Sant\'e Publique, F75012 Paris, France), Nathana\"el Lapidus (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, APHP, H\^opital Saint-Antoine, D\'epartement de Sant\'e Publique, F75012 Paris, France), Daria Bystrova (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, F75012 Paris, France), Benjamin Glemain (Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Sorbonne Public Health Institute, APHP, H\^opital Saint-Antoine, D\'epartement de Sant\'e Publique, F75012 Paris, France, Sorbonne Universit\'e, Inserm, Inria, CNRS, Paris Brain Institute, Paris, France)

item.title: Bayesian Multiple Imputation for Functional Data
item.description: arXiv:2605.08018v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Missing data are pervasive in modern functional datasets, where trajectories are often sparsely or irregularly observed. Although Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) is widely used to reconstruct incomplete curves, existing approaches typically employ single imputation, leading to overly optimistic inferences in downstream analyses. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Bayesian multiple imputation framework for functional data (BAMIFun). For single-level functional data, we impose a Bayesian low-rank model that incorporates penalized spline representations to enforce smoothness of the functional domain and derive an efficient Gibbs sampler algorithm for posterior computation. In addition, we demonstrate and validate how to properly account for estimation uncertainties in downstream analysis. Furthermore, we extend the framework to multiway functional data using Functional Tensor Singular Value Decomposition (FTSVD) model, enabling Bayesian multiple imputation in settings not supported by existing methods. Simulation studies show that BAMIFun achieves substantially improved coverage and more reliable downstream inference compared to existing methods, while maintaining similar imputation accuracy. Case studies using a physical activity dataset and an infant gut microbiome dataset further demonstrate the practical advantages of our proposed methods under severe missingness. The code is available at https://github.com/ZirenJiang/BAMIFun.
item.dc:creator: Ziren Jiang, Lei Xuan, Eric F. Lock, Erjia Cui

item.title: Mixture-of-Finite-Mixtures Wishart Model for Clustering Covariance Matrices with an Application to Brain Functional Connectivity
item.description: arXiv:2605.23207v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data represented as covariance-type matrices arise in many fields, including brain functional connectivity and diffusion tensor imaging. We develop the MFM-Wishart, a Bayesian model-based clustering approach for such data that combines Wishart mixture components with a mixture-of-finite-mixtures (MFM) prior, allowing joint posterior inference on both the number of clusters and clustering assignments. Theoretically, we study the properties of Wishart kernels in the context of mixture models and then establish results for posterior consistency for the number of clusters and posterior contraction of the mixing measure under standard regularity conditions. Computationally, we develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for posterior inference. Simulation studies show competitive clustering performance and accurate recovery of the number of clusters, even under model misspecification. We apply MFM-Wishart to cluster infants based on functional connectivity during sleep, estimated from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data, illustrating the practical utility of the model and revealing interpretable heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Zongyu Li, Stefano Castruccio, Zhiyong Zhang

item.title: Infinite-Dimensional Spherical Kernel ridge Regression
item.description: arXiv:2606.00181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce an intrinsic nonlinear regression framework for responses on a sphere of finite or infinite dimension, viewed as a Riemannian manifold. Unlike traditional tangent-space regressions, which lift responses to a common tangent space and thereby violate intrinsic spherical distances, our proposed method employs an intrinsic approach. We model the intrinsic conditional mean, fitting the responses with respect to the geodesic distance. We use a linear function space as a model space, which we compose with the Riemannian exponential map to obtain predictions on the sphere. Our approach generalises geodesic regression and parametric intrinsic regression models. Leveraging vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory, our approach reduces the infinite-dimensional estimation problem to a finite-dimensional problem via a novel representer theorem, leading to an efficient BFGS-based estimation algorithm. We establish convergence rates and analyse the finite-sample behaviour of our estimator, concluding with an application to density regression. The full implementation is available in R.
item.dc:creator: Beatrice Matteo, Almond Stoecker, Shahin Tavakoli

item.title: A unified approach to outlier identification for mixed-type data
item.description: arXiv:2606.26324v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an outlier identification method for mixed type data sets comprising continuous and ordinal variables. We define outliers based on using a multivariate Gaussian distribution as reference distribution for non-outliers, with a latent Gaussian assumed for ordinal variables. The proposed algorithm is based on the robust Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator for estimating the parameters of the multivariate Gaussian for the non-outliers. This is extended to account for the fact that the full Gaussian information underlying the ordinal variables is not observed. A breakdown theorem shows that replacing observations will noty stop extreme enough outliers from being identified. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated via simulations on synthetic data with various types of contamination, achieving high detection and low false positive rates. Practical relevance is illustrated through an application to Airbnb listing data containing both continuous and ordinal attributes.
item.dc:creator: Efthymios Costa, Christian Hennig

item.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Manifold-Indexed Data
item.description: arXiv:2606.31465v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Functional principal component analysis has traditionally focused on processes indexed by Euclidean domains, although functional observations increasingly arise on curved domains. We develop functional principal component analysis for real-valued processes observed at discrete locations on a general Riemannian manifold. We estimate the mean and covariance functions using intrinsic kernel smoothing based on geodesic distance and a normal-coordinate volume correction, with a general weighting scheme accommodating unequal numbers of observations across subjects. We establish $L^2$ and uniform convergence rates for these estimators and derive corresponding error bounds for the estimated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.
