These results quantify how manifold dimension, sampling frequency and the weighting scheme affect estimation accuracy and characterize the phase transition between sparse and dense sampling regimes. Simulation studies on the circle and sphere, together with real-data applications, illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology.
item.dc:creator: Chang Jun Im, Jeong Min Jeon

item.title: Spectrally Tuned Bandwidth Selection for Kernel Fuzzy Relational Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2607.03117v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fuzzy clustering is used to identify overlapping geometric cluster structures through partial memberships. However, classical methods are limited by the assumption of equal variable importance and by sensitivity to the fuzzifier parameter. These limitations may yield equal cluster membership probabilities, which we refer to as the uniform solution. To address these issues, we propose Kernel Fuzzy Relational Clustering (KFRC) equipped with a bandwidth selection algorithm tuned via the spectral properties of the induced kernel Gram matrix. The KFRC framework implicitly performs unsupervised kernel metric learning by controlling the geometric embedding of the data through adjustable bandwidth parameters. We conduct a formal stability analysis to identify the exact theoretical conditions under which relational clustering collapses, thereby ensuring the stable performance of KFRC. We find that our two-stage bandwidth selection procedure adapts to the data structure while actively avoiding the uniform solution. Furthermore, this theoretical analysis leads to the proposal of a novel fuzzifier function that presents distinct advantages over the power fuzzifier function. We conduct experiments on several synthetic and publicly available data sets to demonstrate that the proposed framework recovers complex structures that traditional methods fail to resolve, while avoiding both uniform and near-crisp solutions.
item.dc:creator: Efthymios Costa, John R. J. Thompson

item.title: A Beta-Based Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator
item.description: arXiv:2607.10905v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive leverage correction for heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimation in ordinary least squares regression. Unlike existing estimators, which rely on predetermined adjustment functions, the proposed approach uses a fitted Beta distribution calibrated to the design matrix's empirical leverage structure. Its parameters are estimated from observed leverage values, allowing the adjustment to reflect the overall configuration rather than individual values alone. The estimator accommodates heterogeneous leverage patterns while avoiding excessive growth of adjustment factors. Monte Carlo simulations show accurate finite-sample inference and confidence interval coverage, alongside desirable asymptotic properties. Empirical applications illustrate its advantages with influential observations and overshooting by existing estimators. The open-source R package hcinfer implements the estimator and related procedures.
item.dc:creator: Marina O. Cunha, Francisco Cribari-Neto, Pedro R. D. Marinho

item.title: Multilevel network meta-regression for multistate models: Population-adjusted joint synthesis of progression and survival from individual and aggregate data
item.description: arXiv:2607.25120v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In network meta-analysis (NMA) of oncology time-to-event outcomes, there is growing recognition that progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) are better synthesized jointly than in separate analyses. The multistate NMA of Jansen et al. addresses this with a tri-state (stable, progressed, dead) Markov model fitted to aggregate survival curves. It cannot, however, adjust for imbalance in effect modifiers across trials, so its relative effects may be biased or not apply to the target population. Multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) resolves covariate imbalance by integrating an individual-level model over each aggregate study's covariate distribution, coherently combining individual participant data (IPD) and aggregate data (AgD); however, for time-to-event outcomes it has been developed only for a single endpoint. This paper introduces multilevel network meta-regression for multistate models (ML-NMR-MS), which embeds the ML-NMR integrated IPD-plus-AgD likelihood inside an illness-death multistate model. For IPD studies the full multistate likelihood over linked transitions is used; for AgD studies covariate-marginal state-occupancy probabilities are computed by quasi-Monte Carlo integration of the occupancies implied by the transition intensities over the reconstructed covariate distribution, and entered through a conditional-survival likelihood. The resulting population-adjusted joint PFS/OS treatment effects can directly parameterize a state-transition economic model. On an illustrative network, ML-NMR-MS resolves a treatment's joint effect into its component transitions, separating an effect on progression from an effect on post-progression survival, and produces conditional and marginal effects. Under correct specification, a simulation study with known truth shows negligible bias and near-nominal coverage for the population-adjusted treatment effects.
item.dc:creator: Jeroen P Jansen

item.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.25304v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulated maximum likelihood is widely used in latent-variable models where likelihood evaluation requires intractable integrals or probabilities. With a fixed number of simulation draws, its estimating equation is generally biased. We develop Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores (SAUSS), combining score simulation with stochastic gradient descent. The Hajivassiliou--McFadden identity, an instance of Fisher's identity, expresses the likelihood score as the conditional expectation of the complete-data score given the observed data. Exact conditional draws yield an unbiased simulated score for any fixed number of draws. The estimator averages stochastic gradient iterates computed using mini-batches of fixed size regardless of sample size, avoiding repeated full-sample likelihood evaluations. Under local regularity and initialization conditions, we establish asymptotic normality and a functional central limit theorem for the partial-sum process of the iterates under multi-pass sampling from an observed sample. These results support plug-in and random-scaling confidence intervals that remain asymptotically valid when algorithmic uncertainty is non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. We develop multinomial probit as a leading application. In simulations and two applications, SAUSS returns estimates in every reported run, including cases where the simulated maximum likelihood implementation returns none. When both return estimates, SAUSS gives comparable estimates in less time.
item.dc:creator: Sokbae Lee, Yuan Liao, Myung Hwan Seo, Youngki Shin

item.title: Partitioning Time in Target Trial Emulation
item.description: arXiv:2609.34576v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In target trial emulation, the treatment strategies that patients follow are inferred from the treatments they actually receive in routine care. However, in most settings, the outcome may preclude the observation of planned treatment, giving rise to immortal time bias through misclassification of treatment strategy, while markers of treatment response may influence subsequent treatment decisions, giving rise to time-varying confounding. A key step toward unbiased treatment effect estimation is to partition follow-up into sufficiently short time intervals to unfold the feedback relationships involving treatment and represent the resulting causal relations with a directed acyclic graph. In this study, we present the possible within-interval causal orderings induced by this partitioning, discuss their causal implications, and assess their plausibility across clinical settings. For each causal ordering, we derive the corresponding g-formula. Using ancestral multi-world networks and simulations, we show that the standard cloning-censoring-weighting estimator is invalid when treatment affects the outcome within a time interval, and we propose a modified version of the method that restores its validity in this setting. Finally, we analyze the consequences of choosing time intervals that are either excessively wide or excessively narrow, thereby formally establishing the need for time partitioning and providing practical guidance for selecting an appropriate partition based on the clinical setting.
item.dc:creator: Harold Tankpinou Zoumenou, Simon Ferreira, Charles Assaad, David Hajage, Fabrice Carrat, Alexandra Beurton, Nathana\"el Lapidus, Daria Bystrova, Benjamin Glemain

item.title: Bayesian Reconciliation of Overlapping Multi Step Forecasts: A Post Processing Framework for Cross Origin Coherence
item.description: arXiv:2610.05340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Overlapping multi step forecasts often disagree, a form of vertical instability that we term cross origin incoherence. We propose a Bayesian reconciliation framework that treats overlapping forecasts as noisy, biased measurements of a common latent trajectory. Operating as a model agnostic post processing layer, it requires no access to model internals. Simulations demonstrate substantial incoherence reduction and robust latent trajectory recovery, remaining highly resilient (correlation 0.972) even under severe nonlinear stress tests. An empirical application to S&P 500 volatility evaluates AR(1), ETS, and LSTM models. The framework reduces incoherence by over 97% across all models while delivering fully calibrated probabilistic forecasts (93% to 94% coverage). Notably, it improves point accuracy for ETS and LSTM. Furthermore, the estimated horizon specific parameters act as a diagnostic X-ray, revealing hidden biases in neural networks without requiring access to their architecture
item.dc:creator: Oluwatosin Bamidele Fajana, Ricardo S. Ehlers, Marinho G. Andrade

item.title: Sharp Partial Identification for Survival Model Comparison Without Target Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.09658v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hospitals often need to know whether a new prognostic model outperforms an established one before survival outcomes in their own patients are available. Without these outcomes, the performance difference is only partially identified: it lies in an interval whose width reflects how far the target population may depart from the source. We show that this interval should be built for the difference itself, not by bounding each model's risk separately, because both risks depend on the same unknown outcomes. For the fixed-horizon Brier-risk difference, under bounded shifts in conditional log-odds that may vary in sign and magnitude across patient profiles, we derive the sharp identified set, prove that it is never wider than separate-risk subtraction, characterize exactly when it is narrower, and give a diagnostic, computable without target outcomes, for when a single-shift model narrows the interval only by assuming homogeneity. Censoring-adjusted simultaneous bootstrap envelopes turn these sets into decisions. Across 32 nonzero-sensitivity comparisons in lung cancer, separate-risk bounds were 4.0-11.1 times as wide as direct identified sets, although sampling uncertainty with 35 source deaths prevented directional certification. In a Rotterdam-to-German Breast Cancer Study Group analysis, direct identification supported the candidate model in a comparison that separate subtraction left inconclusive. Hospitals can thus obtain evidence, before local outcomes exist, on whether a candidate model predicts more accurately under explicitly stated population differences.
item.dc:creator: Won Gi Choi, Sun-Ho Kim, Min Soo Kim

item.title: Clustering extremal dependence structures via Wasserstein distances between angular measures
item.description: arXiv:2610.21931v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Grouping random vectors by their joint extremal behaviour is a recurring task in climate science, hydrology, and finance. Classical clustering is driven by typical observations, while existing extremal procedures either summarize dependence by a single coefficient or discretize the simplex in an ad hoc way. We propose a dissimilarity that compares complete angular measures by optimal transport: each angular measure is estimated above a high radial threshold, mapped from the simplex into a Euclidean space of Aitchison coordinates, and compared by the 1-Wasserstein distance. The methodology is fully nonparametric and requires no fitted model. The dissimilarities feed any distance-based clustering algorithm. Under intermediate-threshold asymptotics and mild moment and separation conditions, hierarchical clustering and partitioning around medoids based on them recovers the latent partition with probability tending to one. In simulations, the proposed approach matches established competitors when clusters differ mainly in the strength of extremal dependence and performs substantially better when equal-strength clusters differ in the shape of their angular measures, especially when asymmetry drives the separation. Applications to rain--snowmelt--runoff extremes in Swiss catchments and to extremal co-movement between international equity markets and the US market reveal hydrologically and economically interpretable groups.
item.dc:creator: Kamal Gasser, Francesco Ragone, Johan Segers

item.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.28910v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.
item.dc:creator: Jose M. Pe\~{n}a

item.title: Weak Factor Recovery in Sparse Bayesian Factor Models under Exchangeable Shrinkage Process Prior
item.description: arXiv:2610.40491v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse Bayesian factor models provide a flexible framework for learning low-dimensional latent structure in multivariate data, but inference on the number of active factors remains challenging when some factors are weak or highly sparse. We study weak factor recovery under a variance based exchangeable shrinkage process (ESP) prior. We derive the posterior factor activation mechanism and show that, conditional on the global and local shrinkage parameters, activation is governed by the standardised loading energy together with the ESP prior activation odds. This yields an explicit activation boundary and clarifies how signal strength, sparsity, the number of observed variables, and the truncation level affect recovery. Simulation experiments show a clear transition between shrinkage and recovery around this boundary and demonstrate that sparsity can substantially affect activation even when raw loading energy is held fixed. They further show that factor activation and recovery of the relative loading pattern across variables can behave differently. These results clarify when weak latent factors become difficult to distinguish from redundant components under ESP shrinkage.
item.dc:creator: Margarita Grushanina

item.title: Private Minimum Hellinger Distance Estimation via Hellinger Distance Differential Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2501.14974v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Objective functions based on Hellinger distance yield robust and efficient estimators of model parameters. Motivated by privacy and regulatory requirements encountered in contemporary applications, we derive in this paper \emph{private minimum Hellinger distance estimators}. The estimators satisfy a new privacy constraint, namely, Hellinger differential privacy, while retaining the robustness and efficiency properties. We demonstrate that Hellinger differential privacy shares several features of standard differential privacy while allowing for sharper inference. Additionally, for computational purposes, we also develop Hellinger differentially private gradient descent and Newton-Raphson algorithms. We illustrate the behavior of our estimators in finite samples using numerical experiments and verify that they retain robustness properties under gross-error contamination.
item.dc:creator: Fengnan Deng, Anand N. Vidyashankar

item.title: Optimal Kernel Learning for Gaussian Process Models with High-Dimensional Input
item.description: arXiv:2502.16617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gaussian process (GP) regression is a popular surrogate modeling tool for computer simulations in engineering and scientific domains. However, it often struggles with high computational costs and low prediction accuracy when the simulation involves too many input variables. For some simulation models, the outputs may only be significantly influenced by a small subset of the input variables, referred to as the ``active variables''. We propose an optimal kernel learning approach to identify these active variables, thereby overcoming GP model limitations and enhancing system understanding. Our method approximates the original GP model's covariance function through a convex combination of kernel functions, each utilizing low-dimensional subsets of input variables. Inspired by the Fedorov-Wynn algorithm from optimal design literature, we develop an optimal kernel learning algorithm to determine this approximation. We incorporate the effect heredity principle, a concept borrowed from the field of ``design and analysis of experiments'', to facilitate efficient computation. Through several examples, we demonstrate that the proposed method provides competitive prediction and variable selection, with favorable computational performance in the examples considered. It is an effective solution for interpreting the surrogate GP regression and simplifying the complex underlying system.
item.dc:creator: Lulu Kang, Minshen Xu

item.title: The Root Finding Problem Revisited: Beyond the Robbins-Monro procedure
item.description: arXiv:2508.17591v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the sequential root-finding problem with repeated noisy measurements. We propose sequential-test bisection STB, which uses a nonparametric sequential sign test to determine when to move to a new design point. Compared with variants of stochastic approximation, STB offers broader adaptivity and faster convergence. When the regression function satisfies $|f(x)|\geq \textsf{c}_0|x-\theta|^\gamma$ in a neighborhood of $\theta$ for constants $\textsf{c}_0,\gamma>0$ where $\theta$ is the root, i.e. $f(\theta) = 0$, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees showing that STB, without using the knowledge of $\gamma$, achieves the minimax adaptive optimal convergence rate $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/(2\gamma)})$, outperforming Robbins--Monro and related stochastic-approximation methods in convergence rate. Under sub-Gaussian noise, STB provides finite-sample confidence sequences for the root $\theta$ without estimating a derivative. In the positive-slope model, we augment STB with {randomized weighted-section and a line fitted to all observations}, leading to asymptotic normality and consistent variance estimation. We formalize the efficiency by a convolution theorem of H\'ajek-Le Cam type. Furthermore, when the regression function is discontinuous at the root, we show that Robbins--Monro converges at rate $1/n$, whereas STB converges super-polynomially. We extend this construction to multivariate nonparametric level-set estimation by sampling along rays. As a technical byproduct, we establish a new central limit theorem under random stopping, with proof techniques that may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Yue Yu, Moulinath Banerjee, Ya'acov Ritov

item.title: Surrogate Modeling and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Complex Systems: A Workflow for Automated Simulation Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2510.16742v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex systems are increasingly explored through simulation-driven workflows that combine physics-based and empirical models with optimization and analytics. Despite their power, these workflows face two central obstacles: high computational cost from repeated expensive simulator runs, and limited transparency when decisions rely on opaque black-box models. We propose a workflow that addresses both challenges by training lightweight emulators on compact designs of experiments that (i) provide fast, low-latency approximations of expensive simulators, (ii) enable rigorous uncertainty quantification, and (iii) support global and local eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) analyses. This work formalizes a methodological bridge accommodating continuous, categorical, and integer variables across diverse domains, from engineering design to socio-environmental agent-based models. To validate surrogate explanations and examine how faithfully they reflect simulator behavior, we introduce a comparative methodology incorporating active validation filters, including explanation consistency and aleatoric uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, we provide practical guidelines for coupling experimental designs with emulator training to select architectures that balance computational efficiency with interpretability. We demonstrate the framework across two contrasting paradigms: a deterministic multidisciplinary design simulation of a hybrid-electric aircraft and a stochastic agent-based simulation of urban segregation. Results show that coupling surrogates with XAI enables large-scale exploration in seconds, reveals critical nonlinear interactions, and highlights potential design and policy levers while establishing consistent explanations across architectures.
item.dc:creator: Paul Saves, Pramudita Satria Palar, Muhammad Daffa Robani, Nicolas Verstaevel, Moncef Garouani, Jordan Levy, Julien Aligon, Benoit Gaudou, Koji Shimoyama, Joseph Morlier

item.title: Inference for Batched Adaptive Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2512.10156v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The advantages of adaptive experiments have led to their rapid adoption in economics, other fields, and among practitioners. However, adaptive experiments pose challenges for causal inference. This note suggests a BOLS (batched ordinary least squares) test statistic for inference on treatment effects in adaptive experiments. The statistic provides a precision-equalizing aggregation of per-period treatment-control differences under heteroskedasticity. The combined test statistic is a linear combination of heteroskedastic per-period z-statistics and can be used to construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals. We provide simulation results comparing rejection rates in the typical case with few treatment periods and few (or many) observations per batch.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kemper, Davud Rostam-Afschar

item.title: Conditioning Gaussian Processes on Almost Anything
item.description: arXiv:2605.21041v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled probabilistic model over functions, but exact inference is restricted to the linear-Gaussian regime. We establish an explicit equivalence between GPs and a class of linear diffusion models, recasting predictive sampling as an ODE with closed-form Gaussian dynamics and a likelihood-dependent guidance term that admits a simple Monte Carlo approximation. In the linear-Gaussian setting, we recover standard GP conditioning exactly; beyond conjugacy, the same machinery handles any conditioning statement admitting point-wise likelihood evaluation - including non-linear physics, and, for the first time, natural language via large language models. Whitening isolates the irreducible non-Gaussian dynamics, minimising Wasserstein-2 transport cost and eliminating numerical stiffness. The result is a general-purpose GP inference scheme requiring no bespoke derivations. Together, these results provide a general mechanism for incorporating the full richness of real-world knowledge as conditioning information, opening a new frontier for the probabilistic modelling of real-world problems.
item.dc:creator: Henry Moss, Lachlan Astfalck, Thomas Cowperthwaite, Colin Doumont, Sam Willis, Philipp Hennig, Christopher Nemeth, Andrew Zammit-Mangion

item.title: Fixed-smoothing Uniform Inference for Quantile Regression
item.description: arXiv:2609.05883v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper develops fixed-smoothing inference methods for time-series quantile regression that are robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. Our approach is uniformly valid over quantile levels and accounts for dependence over time and across quantiles. It enables uniform confidence bands, Wald and Sup-t tests for joint hypotheses, and tests of shape restrictions, providing a unified framework for assessing heterogeneity in quantile effects. Under weak dependence, uniform inference for quantile regression processes is non-pivotal because the limiting distributions depend on the long-run covariance structure across quantiles. To address this issue, we develop two complementary approaches. The uniform-in-$\tau$ method estimates this structure and simulates the non-pivotal limiting distribution. For certain tests involving finitely many quantiles, the stack-Wald method delivers pivotal fixed-smoothing inference. We establish the asymptotic validity of both approaches. Simulations show improved size control over existing HAC-based procedures while maintaining good power. An application to stock-return prediction reveals substantial heterogeneity in predictive effects.
item.dc:creator: Kaicheng Chen, Antonio F. Galvao, Seunghwa Rho, Timothy J. Vogelsang, Jungmo Yoon

item.title: Temporal Seam Score for Assessing Continuity at Known Transitions in Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2609.15132v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long environmental records increasingly combine observations from successive observing or processing systems. Transitions between these systems create temporal seams that may reflect imperfect harmonization or changes in the observed process. We introduce the Temporal Seam Score (S-score, or S), a signed, robust measure for assessing continuity at a known transition time. The complete time series is fitted with a seam-blind model accounting for trend, seasonality, and optional covariates. The residual contrast between symmetric windows around the transition is compared with matched reference contrasts calculated within the contributing segments. The S-score is the standardized departure of the seam contrast from this reference. An S-score near zero indicates that the seam is consistent with ordinary temporal variability. Its sign indicates the direction of the discontinuity, while its magnitude (|S|) indicates how exceptional the discontinuity is. Simulation showed that |S| reflects the imposed discontinuity relative to residual variability: a 20% shift produced a median |S| of 2.58 at a residual coefficient of variation of 0.10, compared with 0.84 at 0.50. In a MODIS-to-Sentinel-3 vegetation record, 121 of 500 sites yielded finite S-scores, of which 90 met all reliability criteria. Among these reliable sites, median S was +0.217 and median |S| was 0.627, indicating little systematic directional displacement and a median seam departure below one reference spread. The S-score provides a general and auditable diagnostic for evaluating temporal continuity across generations of sensors, algorithms, and observing systems without requiring temporal overlap, thereby supporting harmonization quality assurance and more reliable attribution analyses based on long-term environmental records.
item.dc:creator: Hongxiao Jin

item.title: SALE: Source-Aware Dynamic Pricing with Strategic Buyers
item.description: arXiv:2610.22516v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In modern commerce, firms and platforms typically use customer features from different sources to personalize prices: some features are verified using seller records or third-party data, while others are self-reported and may be strategically manipulated by buyers seeking lower prices. In this paper, we study the problem of source-aware dynamic pricing with strategic buyers, where the buyer's valuation is a sparse linear function of her high-dimensional features plus market noise with an unknown distribution. We develop the Source-Aware Localized exploration and calibrated Exploitation (SALE) policy, which personalizes exploration using past learning and verified features, and corrects for strategic manipulation using verified and reported features during exploitation. Our novel personalized design aims to narrow the range of prices explored, reducing unnecessary exploration at excessively high or low prices. To support learning under this design, we derive a new population equation that enables sparse valuation parameter estimation and, in turn, nonparametric estimation of the unknown noise distribution, even when buyer features are dependent over time. By uncovering the intrinsic sparse structure, our analysis establishes estimation guarantees for both learning tasks using the same exploration data. With these guarantees, we show that SALE achieves a sublinear expected regret bound, explicitly quantifying the benefit of using verified features to narrow exploration intervals. Several numerical studies further demonstrate the appealing performance of SALE.
item.dc:creator: Jinjiang Zou, Yang Li, Zemin Zheng

item.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.23570v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent anytime-valid envelopes do, but deterministic ones are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each concerned with a specific algorithm and a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for sharp, data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for a large class of iterative algorithms. Our approach has two key steps: an optimization module derives a one-step recursion that performance measures of many such algorithms satisfy, reducing the error analysis to time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. Then, a statistical module ports the sub-$\psi$ condition to vector-valued processes, uniformly over predictable weights, and derives off-the-shelf boundaries via mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. Combining the two yields readymade envelopes for many iterative algoithms including but not limited to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Oja's algorithm, temporal difference learning, Q-learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD, many with no prior data-adaptive anytime-valid guarantees. Specifically, for SGD, our framework recovers, often under weaker conditions, or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Soham Bonnerjee, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
item.description: arXiv:2610.25667v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two arms for their compliers. Any tilt of assignment toward the reported arm makes reporting the favorite strictly optimal, and no assignment lottery can strictly elicit the ranking below the favorite. We then discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.
item.dc:creator: Tetsuya Kaji

item.title: Time-Uniform Dependent Central Limit Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.29288v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure (FDM) framework. This result yields a universal time-uniform dependent central limit theorem, which serves as the basis for anytime-valid inference. In particular, we instantiate the theorem through asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs), time-uniform counterparts of asymptotic confidence intervals obtained via central limit theorems, extending those originally proposed in Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) to time series with serial dependence. We further refine the original definition because, as we show, it can admit AsympCSs that fail to achieve asymptotic time-uniform coverage even for independent and identically distributed settings. We address this issue by adding a simple eventual-inclusion condition, which in turn permits more flexible variance estimation. In time-series settings, this relaxation can substantially ease restrictions on bandwidth and kernel selection. For feasible implementation of AsympCSs, we establish strong consistency of HAC variance estimators under the FDM framework, accommodating a wider range of commonly used bandwidth choices than existing results under mixing conditions. As illustrations, we construct AsympCSs for algorithms with Markovian structure and time-series-based causal estimands.
item.dc:creator: Mingxuan Ge, Yanlong Liu

item.title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
item.description: arXiv:2610.39194v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). Under such rank-deficient rarity ($n_1 < p$), maximum likelihood estimators suffer from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood methods exhibit severe intercept bias, and convex minority oversampling techniques such as SMOTE collapse into an $(n_1 - 1)$-dimensional affine subspace. In this paper, we propose a novel \textit{Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement} estimator that shifts the paradigm from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Grounded in Stein's Lemma, we prove that the conditional expectation shift of the abundant majority class ($Y=0$) induced by logistic truncation uniquely identifies the true hyperplane normal $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ after Mahalanobis whitening. We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). To accommodate both semi-supervised environments (with an unlabeled background mean) and strictly supervised subsamples, we introduce a hybrid estimator incorporating the intrinsic third-moment skewness of the majority class alongside a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and real-world benchmark applications (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) under extreme rarity ($n_1 \in \{3, 5\}$) demonstrate that our approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth's regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.
item.dc:creator: Chongsun Park
